en: // O // Oṃ, may there be no obstacle! Homage to the perfected one! // O //

Thus, for those who strive to fulfill the duty of a servant desiring to escape from the cycle of birth and death (*janmasaṃsāra*), there exists the venerable *tattvajñāna* (knowledge of reality); that is what you must seek out, for it is superior even to the gods. It is indeed pleasant to know this venerable *tattvajñāna*, for it certainly enables one to perceive the cycle of birth and death and to bring about one’s own liberation. Furthermore, as for what is called the venerable *tattvajñāna*: others say it is Sugata; however, the venerable *tattvajñāna* is also that which serves as the foundation for all principles (*tattva*). Its form is as follows: 1.

Consciousness (*cetana*) and unconsciousness (*acetana*). Consciousness means knowledge, awareness, and mindfulness that does not revert to forgetfulness. Unconsciousness means forgetfulness, delusion, and the absence of mindfulness. That which is consciousness and unconsciousness is called the *śivatattva* and the *māyātattva*. That which is consciousness is the *śivatattva*; that which is unconsciousness is the *māyātattva*. This is according to their gross and subtle aspects. However, the *māyātattva* is eclipsed by the *śivatattva*. The *māyātattva* is neither consciousness nor knowledge; it is merely forgetfulness, lacking the presence of mindfulness, having nothing as its own essence. It is wavering, unstable, and characterized by the forgetfulness of inverted nature. Mindfulness is indeed the luminous nature of the *śivatattva*. That which is called the *śivatattva* has three divisions, namely: *paramaśivatattva*, *sadāśivatattva*, and *ātmikatattva*. 2.

The meaning of *paramaśivatattva* (the principle of Supreme Śiva) is the state of the Lord in the *niṣkala* (partless) condition. He does not act, does not move, does not walk, does not sit, does not lie down, does not appear, does not disappear, and does not vanish. He exists solely as one who is still, tranquil, and serene. He is the origin of all realms; it is said that he pervades all the seven worlds (*saptabhuvana*), from the seven subterranean realms (*saptapātāla*) up to the very summit of the universe. He cannot be perceived by the senses, nor can he be grasped. He is without activity and without purpose. He has no involvement in the affairs of the world. He transcends all these things. Furthermore, for him there is no past, future, or present. He is not affected by time; he is always day and never night. Such are the characteristics of the Lord, the *paramaśivatattva*. This is the state of the Lord in the *niṣkala*; he is indeed the Lord named *paramaśivatattva*. 3.

This is the *sadāśivatattva*; its function is that of Lord *Sadāśivatattva*. "Function" (*vyāpāra*) means that he is honored by the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) and the Maker of All Works (*sarvakāryyakarttā*). As for "Omniscient One" and "Maker of All Works," it is as follows: there exists the *padmāsana* (lotus seat) upon which Lord *Caturśakti* (the Four Powers) resides. Its forms are: *jñānaśakti*, *vibhuśakti*, *prabhuśakti*, and *kriyāśakti*. These are what are called the Four Powers. *Jñānaśakti* has three divisions. Their forms are: *dūradarśana* (seeing from afar), *dūraśravaṇa* (hearing from afar), and *dūrātmaka* (pervasive from afar). *Dūradarśana* means seeing things that are far away. This is what is called *jñānaśakti*. *Vibhuśakti* means that there is no limit to his presence throughout the entire universe. *Prabhuśakti* means that nothing can obstruct his will. *Kriyāśakti* means that he is the creator of this entire universe, even beyond the other deities—such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, the five *ṛṣis*, the seven *ṛṣis*, the divine *ṛṣis*, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vaiśravaṇa, Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Dānavas, Daityas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, Bhūta-dēṅēns, Bhūtakālas, and Bhūta-piśācas; and even beyond these worlds: earth, water, fire, wind, ether, moon, sun, and the hosts of stars. All of these are the works of Lord *Sadāśivatattva* in his aspect as *niṣkala* (without parts). However, the works of Lord *Sadāśivatattva* in his aspect as *sakala* (with parts) include the holy scriptures (*śāstra*), the *āgamas*, sacred teachings (*aji*), medicine (*vaidya*), logic (*tarka*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and mathematics (*gaṇita*). He is the authority (*pramāṇa*) over the entire universe; he is the substance (*dravya*) of both the *sakala* and *niṣkala*. His name is Lord *Ādipramāṇa* (the Original Authority); his name is Lord *Jagannātha* (Lord of the World); his name is Lord *Makarana* (the Cause); his name is Lord *Parameśvara* (Supreme Lord); his name is Lord *Guru* (the Teacher); his name is Lord *Mahulun* (Our Lord); his name is Lord *Vaśavaśitva* (Master of Mastery). All these are his works, though they are not created by him. He is able to bring them forth and able to dissolve them. There is no one who can surpass his sovereignty. He is the Lord, the Teacher of teachers. Such are the characteristics of Lord *Sadāśivatattva*. 4.

Now, that which is called the *ātmikatattva* (the principle of the Self) is Lord Sadāśiva-tattva; as for His characteristic, it is *ūtaprota* (warp and woof). *Ūta* means, for example, like a thread that exists within a cloth; the thread is subtle even while existing within the cotton. In the same way, Lord Sadāśiva-tattva pervades the *māyātattva*; He is not seen and cannot be perceived. He is the pervasive one who permeates the *māyātattva*. *Prota* means, for example, like a crystal gem (*sphatika*) that has been dyed with various colors; though it appears red, it is not actually so. The color becomes as if inherent to the gem because it was dyed with red color by the *māyātattva*. It is not seen and cannot be perceived; He is the pervasive one who permeates the *māyātattva*. When the gem is washed by that very red dye, the cause for the connection between the gem and the color disappears, and it returns to its original form. That former red color existed only within its own interior, and finally [remains] there. In what way is Lord Sadāśiva-tattva pervasive and permeating the *māyātattva*? Impurity (*mala*) is the inherent nature of the *māyātattva*. Therefore, it is called "stained and dyed" (*koparṅga karaktan*), meaning stained by impurity. For this reason, it is as if the power (*śakti*) of the Lord has vanished from within. However, that is not so, because Lord Sadāśiva-tattva is like a crystal; He cannot be defiled. His consciousness itself is dyed by the stain of impurity. The "staining" is produced by the *māyātattva*. Consciousness remains pure and clear; it is omniscient (*sarvajña*) and the doer of all deeds (*sarvakāryakarttā*). His essence remains merely as consciousness. Yet, He is called by the name *ātmikatattva*; He is the Holy Ātman Viśeṣa; He is Lord Dharma. He is the one who permeates all realms; He is the one worshipped by all realms and all beings throughout all births. Such is His manifestation, just like the Holy Sun (*āditya*). He is one, yet His activity is within the interior; His light alone spreads through the ten directions. He permeates all realms, illuminating the good and the bad, the dry and the wet. That light illuminates the good and the bad, the dry and the wet—that light illuminating the good and the bad is the abundant work of the light of the Holy Sun. There is [light] in the bad, there is in the good, there is in the dry, there is in the wet, there is in form and color. The Holy Sun has already performed His task; all the desires of the Holy Sun are contained within Him. In the same way, Lord Dharma eternally exists in the *niṣkala* (partless) state, possessing the *turyapada* (the fourth state) as His essence; His consciousness is eternal.

Even the waters have been dispersed throughout the entire night; this is the dispeller of doubt, reckoned as the life-force of all living beings. That which is called *māyā* is indeed consciousness known as *mañetana*. (5)

"O Lord, please explain the Dharma concerning the nature of consciousness (*cetanā*). O Lord, you yourself desire to know all things; therefore, this is what you wish to hear: the manner in which the Holy Self (*ātmā*) becomes manifest together with the principle of primordial matter (*pradhānatattva*). The *pradhānatattva* is the offspring of the *māyātattva*. This is why the *pradhānatattva* possesses the qualities of forgetfulness (*lupa*) and perversion (*viparīta*). 'Forgetfulness' means being like a human; indeed, the *pradhānatattva* is characterized by forgetfulness. 'Awareness' (*tutur*) and 'clarity' (*prakāśa*) are the characteristics of the Holy Self. That which is both awareness and forgetfulness is called *pradhānapuruṣa*. Upon the union of that *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, there arise the mind (*citta*) and the qualities (*guṇa*). *Mind* (*citta*) is the offspring of the *puruṣa*; *qualities* (*guṇa*) are the products of the *pradhānatattva*. Because of the consciousness (*cetanā*) of the *puruṣa*, the three qualities—whose divisions are as follows: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—are produced. These are called the *triguṇa*. They serve as the qualities of the mind: thus, there is the *sattvic* mind, the *rajasic* mind, and the *tamasic* mind. (6)

*Citta* means the consciousness (*cetanā*) of the *puruṣa* when colored by the agitation of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). *Citta* is the locus; its characteristics are as follows: When *sattva* is predominant, it gathers within that *citta*. Such a person is wise, discerning, and knows what is appropriate and inappropriate, what is noble and what is base, whether with the head or the feet. He is free from pride and conceit; his devotion is sincere, without deceit, and he loves those he loves. He rejoices in the lowly and the poor, and is compassionate toward the suffering. His devotion to truth is firm, and his speech is gentle. He speaks according to the scriptures and the words of the sages. His energy is constant, a quality for attaining right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). He is not forbidden from anything, nor does he feel aversion toward anything. He simply submerges himself in contemplation. All of this brings joy to those who observe him. His voice brings delight to the ears of those who listen. His great power brings satisfaction and contentment to the minds of others. He conforms to their intentions and acts with humility. He does not cause others to suffer for the sake of his own pleasure. He is free from egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and delusion (*moha*), and his activities are driven by sincerity. He merely submerges himself in peaceful conduct, which is naturally unobstructed and never ceases. Thus, his wisdom is his glory and his contemplation is his splendor. This is the manifestation of the *sattva* aspect of the *citta*. These are the characteristics of the *sattva* aspect of the *citta* when it gathers within the *citta*. (7)

Now, these are the characteristics of the *rajas* quality that arise within the mind: it is restless, invisible, and swift in its transformations; it is like iron struck by fire, envious, prone to mocking laughter, reckless, fickle, and impulsive; it is harsh and cruel, devoid of shame or fear, ever-new in its impulses, and causes the body to wither as it gazes about. Its sound causes a piercing pain in the ears of those who hear it; it is impossible to overcome, and its concealment causes distress to the minds of others. It neither reveals nor hides its intentions. Such is the individuality of the *rajas* quality that arises within the mind. (8)

This is the characteristic of the mind in its state of darkness (*tamah*) as it forms within the mind: it is unyielding, deceitful, secretive, and filled with impurity; it is not distressed by the excessive suffering of others; it is dull-witted, deluded, passionate, envious, lustful, and firmly attached to sense objects. Thus it is when the semen and blood have coagulated and matured, becoming the embryo and its limbs. Such is the manifestation of the mind in its state of darkness. This is the characteristic of the mind in its state of darkness as it forms within the mind. 9.

The qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* combine within the mind (*citta*) as the single cause of the *ātman*; thus it attains its own nature. Herein is the sequence of how this occurs: if *sattva* alone is present, the mind becomes luminous; this is the single cause of the *ātman* that attains liberation (*mokṣa*), for *sattva* causes one to experience the essence of the sacred teachings (*āgama*). Therefore, with enthusiasm and effort, one should cultivate the stages of right knowledge (*saṃyajñāna*). If *sattva* meets with *rajas*, the mind becomes luminous; this is the single cause of the *ātman* that goes to heaven (*svarga*). What is this *sattva*? It is the desire to perform good deeds. *Rajas* is that which impels and brings about the fulfillment of the purpose of *sattva*. Such is the function of *rajas*: it leads to heaven through the impulse of *sattva*. When *sattva* meets with *tamas*, the mind becomes luminous; this is the single cause of the *ātman* that becomes a human being. What is this *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* when they are not yet fully manifest? [It is] the desire to perform dharma, merit (*puṇya*), and sacrifice (*yajña*); such is the function of *sattva*. Anger and greed are the function of *rajas*. Secrecy, laziness, and constant delusion are the function of *tamas*. Such are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* when they are not yet manifest. Because they have not yet appeared, there is no virtuous action performed by them; rather, every single act is done erroneously. Such is the principle of how the *ātman* becomes human. Such are the characteristics of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) as they combine within the mind. When the three qualities and the mind meet, the intellect (*buddhi*) arises. The characteristic of the intellect is this: the intellect does not perceive; that which perceives is the intellect. It is as if the intellect does not know, yet it knows; it is as if the intellect lacks consciousness, yet it possesses consciousness. In brief, it is like a flickering light that stands still, rising and falling, always mindful of what is virtuous. Why is it called "intellect" (*buddhi*)? It is because the three qualities are perceived by the mind; that is what is called "intellect. From the intellect arises the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). Ego-sense is the perception of the mind; it is called "consciousness" (*cetana*) or "that which makes conscious. What causes it to be so? Consciousness is the doubt regarding the manifold nature of things; that is why there are many varieties of understanding (*tutur*). Understanding has a manifold and subtle nature. 10.

Now, let the sequence be explained: the Lord within us is the *saṅ hyaṅ ātmā* (the Holy Self); the *saṅ hyaṅ ātmā* makes the *citta* (mind) conscious; the *citta* makes the *ahaṅkāra* (ego) conscious. This [ego] is entered by the *kriyāśakti* (power of action) of the Lord as its means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is called "the life of life," for it is the *kriyāśakti* of the Lord as the means of knowledge, and it serves as the life-force of the *ahaṅkāra* and the life-force of the *buddhi*. That is why it is called the *pramāṇa* of the *ahaṅkāra* and further [of the others], because it manifests the existence of things and their suchness, and it accomplishes all tasks that are truly good. The qualities (*guṇa*) of this *ahaṅkāra* are such that it says: "I am seeing, I am smelling, I am hearing, I am feeling, my body is mine. Such is the speech of the *ahaṅkāra*. The *ahaṅkāra* and the *buddhi* together are called the *viśeṣa-pramāṇa* (specific means of knowledge). Why are the *ahaṅkāra* and the *buddhi* called *viśeṣa*? Because they remain still and inactive, merely reflecting upon what is truly good. The *buddhi* is merely the instrument, and its existence depends entirely upon the *ahaṅkāra*. There are three divisions of it: *si vaikṛta*, *si taijasa*, and *si bhūtādi*. Such is the *ahaṅkāra*. The *ahaṅkāra* that is *si vaikṛta* is the *buddhi* of *sattva*; the *ahaṅkāra* that is *si taijasa* is the *buddhi* of *rajas*; the *ahaṅkāra* that is *si bhūtādi* is the *buddhi* of *tamas*. 11.

From *ga* (the Great Principle) arises one called *vuvusen* (the manifest); this is *ahaṅkāra* (egoism), which is of the nature of transformation (*vaikṛta*). It consists of the mind (*manas*) and the ten faculties (*indriya*). Their types are as follows: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin—these are what are called the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*). Speech, hands, feet, the organ of generation, and the anus—these are what are called the five action-faculties (*pañcakarmendriya*).

The "gross aggregate" (*papiṇḍa*) consists of the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) and the five organs of action (*pañcakarmendriya*); together they are called the ten organs (*daśendriya*). The mind (*manas*) is the eleventh. Such is the function of the *vaikṛta-ahaṅkāra*. As for the *bhūtādi-ahaṅkāra*, its function is the five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*). Their types are: the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*), the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*), the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*), and the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*). Regarding the subtle element of sound: it is that which covers both ears; there exists the sound of a roar. That which is the essence (*liṅga*) of that sound is what is called the subtle element of sound. Regarding the subtle element of touch: there exists wind that blows from the west and strikes [the body]. That which is the essence of that wind—its subtle vibration when it touches—is what is called the subtle element of touch. Regarding the subtle element of form: at twilight, the light of the divine sun (*āditya*) is obscured; there exists the mere essence of its radiance. That which is the essence of that radiance is what is called the subtle element of form. Regarding the subtle element of taste: just as when one eats the six flavors (*ṣaḍrasa*), after having eaten, there remains a mere essence within the mouth. That which is the essence of that taste is what is called the subtle element of taste. Regarding the subtle element of smell: just as when one smells sandalwood or agarwood, the fragrance is faint; there exists a remnant of that scent within the nostrils which is inhaled by the nose. That which is the essence of that scent is what is called the subtle element of smell. (12)

The power of the five *tanmātras* becomes the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*). The element of space arises from the *tanmātra* of sound; its characteristic is that it is intangible, and sound is its quality (*guṇa*). The element of wind arises from the *tanmātra* of touch; its characteristic is that it moves, blows, and strikes when touched by the hand, and touch is its quality. The element of fire arises from the *tanmātra* of form; its characteristic is that it illuminates and burns, and form is its quality. The element of water arises from the *tanmātra* of taste; its characteristic is that it is moist, and the six tastes are its quality. The element of earth arises from the *tanmātra* of smell; its characteristic is that it is solid, and smell is its quality. There are three divisions of smell.
That fragrance is both fragrant and non-fragrant, and it is common to both.

Fragrance is *avaṅ* in the case of something fragrant; it is *abo* in the case of something not fragrant. And that fragrance is common to both; it is neither *avaṅ* nor *abo*. Such is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of earth. That which is the mud of the principle of fire is earth. Earth, water, fire, wind, and space—these are what constitute the worlds of the Lord. Their characteristics are half above and half below, increasing in succession. That principle which is above serves as the quality (*guṇa*) for the principle which is below. Herein lies its characteristic: Space is at the very top; from there arises Wind. This is why the two qualities of Wind are sound and touch. Space, Wind, and Fire—this is why the three qualities of Fire are sound, touch, and form. Space, Wind, Fire, and Water—this is why the four qualities of Water are sound, touch, form, and the six tastes. Space, Wind, Fire, Water, and Earth—this is why the five qualities of Earth are sound, touch, form, the six tastes, and fragrance. 13.

This is the description of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) and their qualities (*guṇa*), which formed the cosmic egg (*aṇḍabhuvana*) by the Lord. Its structure is as follows: there are seven worlds (*saptaloka*) above, and below them are the seven subterranean realms (*saptapātāla*). This is called the "body of the world" (*bhuvanaśarīra*): Satyaloka is at the very top; below that is Mahāloka; below that Janaloka; below that Tapoloka; below that Svarloka; below that Bhuvarloka; and below that Bhūrlloka. Now, Bhūrlloka is the reflection of all the principles (*tattva*). Within Bhūrlloka are the seven mountain ranges, the seven oceans, the seven continents, the ten winds, and the ten senses. All these together constitute the state of delusion (*samoha*) within Bhūrlloka. The seven mountain ranges have earth as their constituent substance (*rakṣaṇa*), which is the intermediate realm (*bhuvanāntara*). The seven oceans have water as their constituent substance, which is the intermediate realm. The seven continents have fire as their constituent substance, which is the intermediate realm. The ten winds have air as their constituent substance, which is the intermediate realm. The ten senses have ether (*ākāśa*) as their constituent substance, which is the intermediate realm. Such is the description of all the principles that are deluded within Bhūrlloka. Now, as for the seven subterranean realms (*saptapātāla*): Pātāla, Vaitala, Nitala, Mahātala, Sutala, Talātala, and Rasātala. At the bottom of the seven subterranean realms is Balagarddabha Mahānaraka (the Great Hell of the Ass-Headed Demons). At the bottom of Mahānaraka is where the divine Kālāgnirudra (the Rudra of the Fire of Time) dwells, who is always ablaze. For one hundred thousand *yojana* in extent, the divine Kālāgnirudra’s fire spreads out, consuming the seven subterranean realms. Such is the description of the cosmic egg. It is layered upon one another like the layers of a palm fruit, according to the number of the principles. Thus is the extent of the work of the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) known as *bhūtādi*, which is its root. (Verse 14)

What are the characteristics of the *taijasa* ego (*ahaṅkāra*)? It is one that is like the wind; its characteristic is turbulence. The *vaikṛta* and *bhūtādi* [types of ego] combine to produce the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Furthermore, the three types of ego have the same characteristics as the intellect (*buddhi*); they approach it through the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. What is meant by "approaching"? The venerable one called *pramāṇa* (the means of knowledge) is the Lord Ātman who exists in the state of *tūryapada*. He is the one who is grasped as the venerable *pramāṇa*; he is the one who acts, performing the purification of auspicious actions. Furthermore, the intellect, mind, and ego serve as the instruments for the venerable *pramāṇa* to act and purify auspicious effects. Such are the characteristics of the venerable *pramāṇa* with the intellect, mind, and ego as its instruments. What is the distinction between *pramāṇa* and *viśeṣa*? Herein lies their difference: regarding the Ātman, there are two of them, yet there are two distinctions. The venerable *pramāṇa* is distinguished from the *viśeṣa*. The venerable *pramāṇa* is active in auspicious matters, whereas the venerable *viśeṣa* is inactive, having no purpose or function in auspicious matters. It merely remains in a state of stillness—neither moving, nor acting, nor behaving, nor striving. Such are the characteristics of the venerable *pramāṇa* and *viśeṣa*, which are mutually dependent. Thus ends the discussion of what is called *pramāṇa*. Regarding the Ātman, there are two of them, and these states themselves possess distinctions. Doubt is the basis upon which the venerable Ātman relies; this is what the Ātman follows. The inherent nature of the Ātman is such that the Ātman exists in the state of *tūryapada*, which is precisely the *pramāṇa* and *viśeṣa* in their ultimate form. When the venerable Ātman descends into the waking state (*jāgrapada*), that is the *pramāṇa* in its manifest form. When the venerable Ātman descends into the sleeping state (*suptapada*), that is likewise so. Such is the reality: the venerable Ātman remaining in a state of stillness is called *viśeṣa*; when the venerable Ātman is active in purifying, that is what is termed *pramāṇa*. Such are the characteristics of the venerable Ātman across all states; the *pramāṇa* and *viśeṣa* are indeed one and the same. How is it that the ego is called *pramāṇa*? Because it serves as the instrument for that very act of purification. Furthermore, the reason why there appear to be three forms of the intellect is because the threefold ego provides the support for the intellect. Thus, the threefold intellect increases to fifty; the fiftyfold intellect increases to six thousand; the six-thousandfold intellect increases to ten thousand; the ten-thousandfold intellect increases to... (and so on).
Therefore, do not disregard it; for this is the cause of the soul's elevation. 15

The *mapa kari* (the maker of the world) consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. These determine whether one goes to heaven, hell, the human realm, or the animal realm (*tiryak*). Such is the teaching of the other [scriptures]. However, here [it is said]: the threefold *ahaṅkāra* is the progenitor of the *buddhi*. There is the *buddhi* of *sattva*, the *buddhi* of *rajas*, and the *buddhi* of *tamas*. These cause one to attain their respective wombs (*yoni*), which serve as one’s birthplace. One who knows the subtle reality (*nipuṇatattva*) understands that this is the sequence. Therefore, one must discern those wombs that grant liberation (*mokṣa*) and heaven, as well as those births that are repeatedly subject to decay. This sequence shall now be explained. If there is a *buddhi* of *sattva* that is intense in its characteristic of wisdom (*prajñāna*) and seeks to destroy ignorance through the study of the scriptures, then the womb of *sattva* is that of the *tripuruṣa* (the three divine beings). If there is a *buddhi* of *sattva* that is intense in its characteristic of asceticism (*brata*), austerity (*tapa*), yoga, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), then the womb of *sattva* is that of the *pañcaṛṣi* (the five sages). If there is a *buddhi* of *sattva* that is intense in its characteristic of worship (*pūjā*), adoration (*arcana*), recitation of mantras (*japa*), and praise (*stuti*) of the Lord, then the womb of *sattva* is that of the *saptaṛṣi* (the seven sages). If there is a *buddhi* of *sattva* that does not seek its own welfare but has compassion for all living beings, then the womb of *sattva* is that of the *devaṛṣi* (the celestial sages). If there is a *buddhi* of *sattva* that is intense in its characteristic of courage (*kadhīra*), heroism (*kavanin*), and bravery (*kaśūra*), which is not faint-hearted regarding the sacrifice of life, even unto death, so that one may offer one’s body as a means to fulfill one’s devotion; which is full of aesthetic delight (*rasika*) yet free from delusion, whose activity is directed solely toward the goal, and whose mind is entirely peaceful and unwavering when practicing courage and heroism—then the womb of *sattva* is that of the *vidyādhara*. If there is a *buddhi* of *sattva* that is intense in its characteristic of joy (*kalaṅön*), which experiences daily delight that is pleasing to the ear and firm in the heart, which is steadfast in the pursuit of whatever is beautiful, and whose joy is such that it gazes at everything with a flickering eye—then the womb of *sattva* is that of the *gandharva*. Thus, these are not the grounds upon which true knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) can destroy the state of bondage to reach the path of liberation. However, those that are fit to be the grounds for true knowledge do indeed attain liberation, namely the states of the *ṛṣi*, *devaṛṣi*, *saptaṛṣi*, *pañcaṛṣi*, and so forth, beginning with the *tripuruṣa*. Such, then, are the *buddhi* of *sattva* in its lowest, middling, and highest forms. (16)

There is a *buddhi* characterized by *rajas* that perceives improper sounds; there is anger, and furthermore, it is prone to dying. It does not fear the glare of a flash of lightning; its cause is the provocation of others, and for that reason, it likewise destroys its own body. With its very essence within its heart, it becomes liquid and produces tears. Such is the *rajas*-born *yoni* of the *dānava*. There is a *buddhi* characterized by *rajas* that perceives improper sounds; there is anger, and furthermore, it is prone to being agitated. It dwells in the upper part of the body. It speaks thus, saying: "I have the authority to utter even improper words, just as one might speak with various gestures; furthermore, when engaged in debate, I shall strike my opponent. Such is the *rajas*-born *yoni* of the *daitya*. There is a *buddhi* characterized by *rajas* that perceives improper sounds, whose bodily form is entirely covered in dust. Its speech is restless, its hands are restless, and its feet are restless; it makes a loud noise, shouting and making others shout along with it, without heeding the words of others. Such is the *rajas*-born *yoni* of the *rākṣasa*. Now, regarding the reality (*tattva*) of the *rākṣasa*: it is the deity of the sword and the weapon of the Lord (*prabhu*). Of all swords currently existing, the *rākṣasa* is the life-force (*ātmā*) and its presiding deity (*devatā*). The *daitya* is the deity of the sword and the weapon of the farmer, like the blade of a sickle. Of all swords, the *daitya* is the means (*sādhana*) for producing crops and its presiding deity. The *dānava* is the deity of the sword and the weapon of the ascetic (*viku*), like a small knife or a ritual dagger (*karayu*); the *dānava* is its presiding deity. Such are the *buddhi* types of *rajas*: the lowest (*kaniṣṭha*), the middle (*madhyama*), and the highest (*uttama*). 17.

If one chooses the food [appropriate] for the *buddhitamas* (the darkness of the intellect), that *buddhitamas* will carry it away. When it has eaten the food of the *gaṅan* (the body), which consists of the skin, flesh, and blood, its mind becomes satisfied. Its birthplace is among the *bhūtas* and *yakṣas*. Its location is in the hollows; it is made into the *dhātus* (elements) of the hollows, such as the *liṅga*, the image, and the *liṅgin* who performs worship. But when the *buddhitamas* does not choose the food, it does not conform to its desire. It is restless, lacking self-control, and its mind is neither focused nor collected. If it obtains enjoyment (*bhoga*), it is excessive; its mind is like the *bhūta* whose birthplace is darkness. Its location is in the hollows, deep within the limbs; it is made into the wood and plants of the forest. When the *buddhitamas* is satiated by the food, it does not reject anything according to its own preference. All the meat it eats is considered mixed with its food; thus says the scripture. Its birthplace is the *bhūta* of Time (*kāla*). Its location is in the hollows, at the crossroads where the four paths meet. If the *buddhitamas* does not eat, is not pleased, and is the cause of distress, it wanders toward the west and the south. It does not hesitate, and it knows the vulnerabilities of others. It uses this as a sign to cause harm and to bring about misfortune. It is focused on the *tañjakan* (the point of contact); it listens intently to its ears in order to perceive enjoyments. Its birthplace is the *piśāca* spirit. Its location is in the sky; its behavior is erratic and unsteady. This is what is called *sasabāvuh* (the state of being blown about). Thus says the world. Such are the *buddhitamas* in its lowest, middling, and highest forms. These—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—are the causes of the soul’s various states. Such is the sequence; thus it should be understood. (18)

When the *bhūtayakṣa* element meets with gods, celestial sages (*devaṛṣi*), the seven sages (*saptarṣi*), the five sages (*pañcarṣi*), and the three persons (*tripuruṣa*), it manifests as the intellect (*buddhi*). This is the cause by which the self (*ātman*) attains liberation (*mokṣa*). Furthermore, when the *bhūtadeṅĕn* element meets with *daityas*, *mātras*, *vidyādharas*, and deities (*devatā*), it manifests as the intellect. This is the cause by which the self attains heaven (*svarga*). Furthermore, when the *bhūtakāla* element meets with *rākṣasas* and *gandharvas*, it manifests as the intellect. This is the cause by which the self becomes human (*mānuṣa*). Furthermore, when the *bhūtapiśāca* element meets with *rākṣasas*, it manifests as the intellect. This is the cause by which the self falls into hell (*naraka*). Furthermore, when the *bhūtapiśāca* exists alone, it manifests as the intellect. This is the cause by which the self becomes an animal (*triya*). Thus, one should know the various manifestations of the noble self (*saṅ hyaṅ ātmā*). There is doubt regarding the number of the noble "three persons" (*tripuruṣa*). The term "three persons" refers to Lord Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara; they are the primordial essence (*ādisattva*). That primordial essence, through negligence, transforms into the five sages (*pañcarṣi*); the five sages transform into the seven sages (*saptarṣi*); the seven sages transform into celestial sages (*devaṛṣi*); the celestial sages transform into deities (*devatā*); the deities transform into *vidyādharas*; the *vidyādharas* transform into *gandharvas*; the *gandharvas* transform into *dānavas*; the *dānavas* transform into *daityas*; the *daityas* transform into *rākṣasas*; the *rākṣasas* transform into *bhūtayakṣas*; the *bhūtayakṣas* transform into *bhūtadeṅĕns*; the *bhūtadeṅĕns* transform into *bhūtakālas*; the *bhūtakālas* transform into *bhūtapiśācas*; and the *bhūtapiśācas* transform into humans (*mānuṣa*). The human state is not yet reached by the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), for it is the foundation of both the auspicious and the inauspicious. When the deity descends into the human power, the nature of the deity is still obscured. From the human, it transforms into animals (*triya*). There are five kinds of animals: the quadruped (*pāśu*) found in the village; the wild beast (*mṛga*) found in the forest; the bird (*pakṣī*) found in the air; the fish (*mīna*) found in the water; and the insect (*pipīlikā*), which refers to beings that crawl on the ground. Furthermore, there are those that are known as "creeping things" (*sarīsṛpa*), those that move by slithering, and the immobile (*sthāvara*) which remains fixed in the earth. Such are the transformations of the noble self when it is a human being who has become negligent.
Yoga // 19

Furthermore, it is said that suffering is experienced by the noble *ātman*. It is as if it were submerged and vanished, not remaining within its own nature (*jāti*). It is as if the noble *ātman* were not distressed; it falls [into a state] like the trembling of a Java vine when shaken. Then it is carried away by others to the ocean, where it remains for a very long time within its own nature in Java. Such is the noble *ātman*: when it has already become a god (*triya*), it suffers because of having been an animal, for it is fit to be the means (*sādhana*) for performing good deeds. When it becomes an ant, it is like the head of a flea—biting, scratching, stinging, and biting—all of which are things disliked by humans; it is even more so when it is crushed. Furthermore, among the gods, there are those who are to be honored and those who are to be disliked. What is the meaning of this? It is the karma of evil: inferior, middling, and superior. What is the inferiority of one who performs evil? It is when a person is clouded by anger, becoming reckless and impulsive. Such is the manifestation of their performance of evil; they fall into hell, where their suffering is intense. When their lifespan there ends, they are given birth as a human by the servants of Yama (*yamabala*). Their form is not like that of a virtuous person; this is what is called "birth through transformation" (*vikārajanma*). This is a state of mutilation; all such mutilations are the fruit of the inferiority of one's actions. // 20 //

Kill this person; in the midst of his body, evil is found, caused by the desire for wealth. His eyes are his axe; such is the reason evil is found within him. He constantly seeks out the vulnerabilities of the virtuous. For that reason he acts thus; he casts away his own welfare in this manner. He shall fall into hell. When he has reached hell, he is given birth as a beast by the power of Yama. Yet even that beast may be eaten; it may be eaten as the means for performing sacrifices and cultivation. Such is the result of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This is the nature of the fruit of his evil deeds. // 21 //

This is the supreme result of one’s evil deeds. Indeed, it is caused by his egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), by greed (*lobha*), by delusion (*moha*), by hypocrisy (*dambha*), and by a lack of shame and modesty (*ahirīkya-anapatrāpya*). His knowledge is not pure and true; he commits evil with a corrupted heart, yet he does not feel remorse; he remains unashamed even when confronted by others; he gives harsh rebukes to others, eats the food of others, and takes what belongs to them. Such is the sequence of that birth; at all times it is experienced, endured, and felt by all human beings. Whatever they have sown, according to their own actions, is what is reaped. Alas, such a person, in due course, will not long remain before descending to hell. Upon emerging from there, he is made into an animal by the servants of Yama. This is its essence: all the various births of animals are experienced, endured, and felt by humans as the very fruit of their own births. Such is the fruit of the supreme evil deed. Conversely, the opposite is true: there is no doubt regarding the birth of the noble self (*ātman*). One must clearly understand the distinctions within one’s own heart. If there is a path, one may indeed reach the state of the lowest [births] through the wisdom of the learned. What is the cause of the five types of animal births? It is because humans commit the three kinds of evil deeds. That is why they are born as such among humans; that is why they are born as animals. If others speak thus, [the answer is: Indeed, this world arises in this manner. These five types of animals—neither heaven nor hell—are included within all births, both good and bad, which serve as the offerings for the destination of the world. Heaven is the fruit of performing good deeds; hell is the fruit of performing evil deeds. Upon emerging from there, if one is born as an animal, it is because the return is the result of evil deeds. In short, both the good and the bad are the offerings for the world. Thus we wander through these three realms, experiencing pleasure and pain, old age, sickness, death, and birth. Such is the offering of birth. There is no other way. Therefore, there is no doubt in us, for the world is the offering of the Lord (*Bhaṭāra*). We die and are born again; such is our nature. (22)

Indeed, this is the essence of the noble knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which has been presented to you all; for that is the cause, that is the means by which the various realms (*rāt*) are manifested. If you understand it, you will experience it; you will perceive the flavor of the noble knowledge of reality. When the noble knowledge of reality is fully realized, it transcends the realms; such is the meaning of its teaching. It brings forth the flavor of the application of the union (*prayogasandhi*), through the guidance of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), the observance of the stages (*bhūmyabrata*), austerity (*tapa*), yoga, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This is the path for the soul’s liberation from the cycle of rebirth (*ātmasaṃsāra*). // 23 //

The *ātman* does not cause the perception of *saṃsāra*. It is only when one has attained the knowledge of the supreme reality (*tattvajñāna*) that it ceases. This is because the state of the divine *ātman* exists within the *tūryyapada*; once the Lord has awakened, He is called the Pervasive One (*vyāpī*), existing within the partless (*niṣkala*). The power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the Lord is the penetration of *umā* into the *ahaṅkāra*; the *ahaṅkāra* penetrates the *vāyu*; that *vāyu* enters into the *nāḍī*; and that *nāḍī* is subtle within the body. That body is what perceives the five destinies of *saṃsāra*, yet its necessity is determined by the Lord. As for that which perceives *saṃsāra*, if it is thus, it becomes a threefold animal. If others speak in this way, it is indeed true; however, here is an illustration based on direct observation, like the case of a swordsmith (*paṇḍe vusi*). A sword is made by him; though it is a single object, its manifestations are many: there is the axe, the chisel, the file, the saw, and the blade—all are but swords, yet they are designated differently. Just as a sword is made by a swordsmith, so too is the sword of many kinds: there is the sword used as a weapon by a ruler, the sword used as a weapon by a commoner, and the sword used as a weapon by a scholar (*paṇḍita*). Yet all are simply swords, regardless of their names. As long as the sword is still being forged, it is merely called a "sword"; its function depends entirely on the smith. The sword held by the ruler is like a chisel: it is sharp and serves as the instrument for the ruler to obtain his livelihood. The sword held by the commoner is like a hoe or a spade: it serves as the instrument for those who live by manual labor. The sword held by the scholar is like a small knife, a razor, or a lancet: it serves as the instrument for those who seek wisdom. Yet, it is the sword alone that reaches the highest goal; whereas the other tools do not reach the highest goal, for they are merely instruments for their respective tasks. Once the scholar has finished his work, he is pervasive and all-encompassing; it is the will of the scholar’s mind that fashions the various tools. The scholar alone knows the product of the tool and employs it as an instrument for his own perception, using the tools as his means of action. Even the tools themselves, when employed by the scholar, are deluded; if the scholar is absorbed in the Supreme, the tools are also absorbed. Their existence lies within His command. (24)

Listen, O noble ones! Such is our Lord. He is indeed all-pervasive; His consciousness alone brings forth all these births. This is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of our Lord, which causes the self (*ātman*) to exist in the state of *tūryapada* (the fourth state), as well as the self that exists in the state of *jāgrapada* (the waking state), and causes the self to exist in the state of *suptapada* (the sleeping state). Through this, He oversees the five destinies of *saṃsāra*: pleasure and pain, birth and death, prosperity and decline, and the cycle of existence. In brief, the self that undergoes *saṃsāra* is brought forth by our Lord. Now, let the sequence be understood: Our Lord, the Great Seer, perceives all things. That is why the self desires Him—He who is singular, for there is no other form of the Holy Self. At the time when He is desired by our Lord, He is made to become conscious within the *pradhānatattva*. However, in that state, the Holy One remains distinct; He possesses both activity (*vyāpāra*) and non-activity. "The self has activity" means: at the time when He is made conscious within the *pradhānatattva* by our Lord, "becoming conscious" means that He exercises His own intelligence. To perceive, to reflect—that is what is called "becoming conscious. 25

The *ātman* is its activity (*vyāpāra*). The Lord (Bhaṭara) causes it to descend; He comes to consume and to provide consciousness. When that *ātman* descends, it comes to possess consciousness, just as in the previous example of the ascetic’s body: the body descends [into animation]. Such is the characteristic of the Holy *Ātman*: it comes to be made conscious by the Lord; the Holy *Ātman* descends and becomes conscious. In the state of isolation (*kaivalya-sthiti*), it remains still, without activity and without agitation; it is called the *Ātmaviśeṣa*. It is also known as Bhaṭara Dharma. However, at the time of its activity of providing consciousness, it is further known as *Pramāṇa*. This *Ātman* is called the Holy *Pramāṇa*, together with the Holy *Ātmaviśeṣa*. In the state of absolute oneness (*kevala-sthiti*) it exists in the *tūryapada* (the fourth state); however, this *Ātman* exists in the *jāgrapada* (the waking state). Thus, their characteristics are indeed one and the same. What is the characteristic of the *Ātman* existing in the *tūryapada*, while there is a difference between the two? That [difference] is subtle and beyond counting. The *Ātman* existing in the *jāgrapada* has consciousness (*cetana*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Consciousness means that the *Ātman* in the *tūryapada* is beyond counting. That which is called *citta* is that which is colored by the three qualities (*triguṇa*). *Citta* means the faculty of cognition (*tutur*) whose activity (*vyāpāra*) does not know the supreme good. That cognition and *citta* have one and the same intrinsic nature. *Citta* is activity; *tutur* is its state when it remains still and inactive. This *Ātman* existing in the *jāgrapada* is one in its cognition and activity, and also in its non-activity. The distinction between them is simply a matter of naming; it is the *Ātman* itself. This *Ātman* is fashioned so that it may experience the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) with its joys and sorrows. This *Ātman* is called *ahaṅkāra*; this is what is fashioned by the Lord to produce various doubts. This is the faculty of cognition (*prabot*) of the *Ātman* existing in the *jāgrapada*, as well as of the *Ātman* existing in the *tūryapada*; these are the works of the Lord. Such is the sequence to be understood. The *Ātman* called *ahaṅkāra* of the *vaikṛta* type is fashioned by the Lord along with the ten sense organs (*daśendriya*). Furthermore, the *Ātman* called *ahaṅkāra* of the *bhūtādi* type is made by the Lord to fashion the five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*) and the five gross elements (*pañcamahābhūta*). As for the *manas* (mind), *manas* means perception (*hiḍep*). That perception is further constructed so that the *Ātman* may produce various manifestations. The *Ātman* that produces these is called the *ātmaparivāra* (the retinue of the *Ātman*). The *ātmaparivāra* consists of the following types: *Ātman*, *Parātmā*, *Nirātmā*, *Antarātmā*, and *Sūkṣmātmā*. These are the five *Ātmans*. Their perception is one and the same; this is called the "measure" (*pamkas*) of the *Ātman*.
O Gaṇal, you alone have understood the essence of the supreme good; you have not merely mastered the conventional ways.
(26) The primary matter (*pradhāna*) is like a cart, the person (*puruṣa*) is like a bull, and the Lord (*īśa*) is joined as the charioteer; thus the world revolves like a turning wheel. (27)

The *pradhāna-tattva* is like a cart; the *ātman* is like a bull; and Lord *Īśvara* is like the charioteer. When the *ātman* is driven by the *grītan* (the senses), it wanders through the world like a spinning wheel. This world is like the wheel of a revolving millstone that revolves and grinds the gods, humans, and animals, caused by the force of their good and evil *karman*. Such is the nature of the *ātman* when it is associated with the *guṇas*. When the *ātman* possesses the sword, it is like a swordsman; when the *ātman* is active (*vyāpāra*) in the fourth state (*tūryapada*), it is like a master swordsman. But when the *ātman* is not active, it is merely the weapon of the swordsman. The *ātman* in the waking state and the *ātman* in the fourth state do not yet fully attain the state of goodness (*halahayu*). We have already explained this to you, O Lord: He is all-pervading and omnipresent; His will is constant, and He brings about all births. Now, as for the *ātman* called "dwelling in *saṃsāra*": others say it is the *ātman* dwelling in *saṃsāra*, but the *ātman* referred to here is the *ahaṅkāra* of the *vaikṛta* type; its intellect (*buddhi*) is *sattva*, and it experiences pleasure. The *ātman* called the *ahaṅkāra* of the *taijasa* type has an intellect of *rajas* and experiences pain. The *ātman* named the *ahaṅkāra* of the *bhūtādi* type has an intellect of *tamas* and is made to experience pain. (28)

Now, let us distinguish the Self (*ātman*) that is sought after from the Self that is not sought after. What indeed is that which is the Lord Dharma? It is He who is the life of all living beings. The Lord has already been born among us; it is He who returns again to take birth, the very life of life. Truly, O Lord, He exists as the life of every person. However, His characteristics are woven like warp and woof. "Warp" (*ūta*) means, for example, like fire that exists within dry wood: though not yet recognized and not yet visible, its existence is both manifest and unmanifest. What is meant by this? It is like dry wood that has been struck by lightning; it is destined not to produce fire, because it is unfit to produce fire, since it is already saturated with fire. 29. *Nihan ta prabhedanyātmā maṅhiḍĕp / lavan ikaṅ ātmā tan paṅhiḍĕp / apa pva ya mataṅnyan bhaṭara dharmma / an sira pinakahurip niṅ sarvvajanma kabeh / tlas karuhun bhaṭara mahulun / an sira rakva tumut maṅjanma / pinakahurip niṅ hurip // siṅgih bhaṭara hana pinakahurip niṅ voṅ kabeh / ndan ūtaprota lakṣaṇanira / ūta ṅaranya / kady aṅga niṅ apuy hana ri ṅĕsĕyĕn / priṅampyal kayu / kunaṅ tan kinavruhan / tan katon juga hananya / vyakta tan vyakta juga hananya / apa kaliṅanya / ya ta ṅara ṅĕsĕyĕṅ vaṅi rikaṅ priṅampyal kayu / niyatanyan tan pamijilaknapuy / kaṅ yogya mijilaknapuy / apanegĕh kaṅ kinahanan de niṅ apuy //* 29. The Lord has already been born among us; it is He who returns again to take birth, the very life of life. Truly, O Lord, He exists as the life of every person.
