This is the meaning of the *taliṅ* (the essential teaching): How is it with the Lord (*bhaṭara*)? He is the cause of all births; he is both manifest (*vyakta*) and unmanifest (*tan vyakta*). He exists throughout all time. This is his dwelling place, both in the manifest and the unmanifest; he exists within all people. All births are indeed empty of speech and devoid of that which can be known through them. That which is grasped by means of speech and knowledge—that is what is described here. He who has already mastered the application of the *sandhi* (union) of the *prayoga*, furthermore, is one who has perfected *tapa* (asceticism), *vrata* (vows), *yoga*, and *samādhi*. What is the reason that such a person is able to cultivate *jñāna* (knowledge) and is capable of attaining the specific states of *yoga*? Its benefit is this: in its entirety, he knows *yoga* and *samādhi*; he has perfected *tapa*, *vrata*, *yoga*, and *samādhi*. He is capable of fulfilling every desire, and he alone is capable of accomplishing his own purpose. Of all these...

The *lumkasaknikaṅ* is the conjunction of practice (*prayogasandhi*). It is not merely knowledge alone, because it is supported by what is called the *ātmāviśeṣa* (the supreme self), which is that which is worshipped by the Lord. Indeed, your understanding is like the brilliance of a gem; its location is in one place, yet such is the Lord. He exists as one who occupies a single location. Furthermore, he who is worshipped by the Lord is indeed spiritual (*ādhyātmika*). There is no need for vows, asceticism (*tapa*), yoga, or meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Why? Because they do not have that name. That which is repeatedly practiced in such a manner is not it, because he is that which is supported by the *ātmāviśeṣa*, and he is that which is worshipped by the Lord. Thus says the *Agama*: "If it is so, what does the opponent say? Is it false? No, for these—vows, asceticism, yoga, and meditative absorption—are indeed necessary. What is this meditative absorption? It is *īśvarapraṇidhāna* (devotion to the Lord). This is the means of attaining the holy *ātmāviśeṣa*, and furthermore, the means of attaining the Lord. When one has already begun to practice, that meditative absorption is *īśvarapraṇidhāna*. It does not diminish or waver; his life is entirely absorbed in practicing that meditative absorption. Even in his final birth, he continues to practice that meditative absorption. And so it is said by the Lord: he is worshipped by the Lord. In brief, when he is attained through the attainment of meditative absorption, he exists within him; that is not an attainment, nor is it meditative absorption. He does not exist within him. Now, regarding the five senses (*pañcatriyak*): they are considered to be the fire of the Lord’s Dharma. Why is it that their nature is contrary to what is said? Its benefit is that it explains all purposes. If it is true, it is supported by the Lord Dharma. Why would it act otherwise? That is the basis for inference, that the Lord is present there. It is not merely not supported; its essence is the *ātmāviśeṣa*. Where is that *ātmā* located? The *ātmā* is indeed pervasive. That is the manifestation of the *ātmā* in its manifoldness. That which is perceived through consciousness—by that, the vital air (*vāyu*) exists. Sound (*śabda*) is also consciousness; it exists there. The vital air is its life-force; consciousness is what is desired; sound is its resonance. Therefore, sound is not a material thing (*avastu*) among the senses, because it is not supported by the *ātmāviśeṣa*. However, the vital air, sound, and consciousness are the remnants of the cycle (*vratta*). In the three worlds—among the stationary (*sthāvara*) and the moving (*jaṅgama*), in grass, trees, creepers, shrubs, and bushes—there is no lack of vital air, sound, and consciousness. These are the beings that grow. But as for those..."
The self is indeed distinct; it simply has no location, yet it forgets its characteristics during this birth. // 30 //

Wind, sound, and touch are likewise present in all births—whether human, inferior (kaniṣṭha), middling (madhyama), or superior (uttama). However, the noble *ātmāviśeṣa* (the specific Self) is purely internal (*ādhyātmika*). That which is honored as the specific Self is that which has been realized by us, the Lord, through worship. All human beings possess it; they do not lack it, whether they have memory, forgetfulness, wisdom (*prajñā*), or ignorance. What is meant by this? It is that which is honored by the specific Self: wisdom, memory, and so forth. What is this "memory"? It is the awareness of the noble specific Self. Now, among humans, there are those who possess wisdom and those who possess memory; these are the inferior, the middling, and the superior. How is it so? What is the distinction between inferior, middling, and superior? It is the characteristic of the noble Self as it manifests in human birth. Because of this, there are the inferior, the middling, and the superior. Such is the nature of those with memory and wisdom. As for those who are ignorant and forgetful, their memory is slight; they are the "inferior of the inferior. This is what is called the Self when it is thus. This is the reasoning for the births of the inferior, middling, and superior, according to whether one possesses wisdom and memory. What is the Self that is inferior, middling, or superior? Its characteristics exist in the waking state (*jāgrat-pada*) and exist in the fourth state (*tūrya-pada*). If the Self is superior, it exists in a person who possesses wisdom and memory; such a person is superior. If the Self is middling, it exists in a person whose possession of wisdom and memory is middling. But if the Self is inferior, it exists in a person whose possession of wisdom and memory is inferior. If the Self is the "inferior of the inferior," it exists in a person who lacks both wisdom and memory; in such a case, there is merely the capacity for speech. There are people who are like this. However, those who are honored by the specific Self are superior; they indeed possess the superior Self, and that is what is called the "specific Self" (*ātmāviśeṣa*). Yet, even so, there is a difference in the degree to which they are honored by the specific Self; it is not that the specific quality itself is different. All things are [subject to] this, but there is further distinction in the body and its components. It is the good and evil karma (*śubhāśubha-karma*) that produces these states; this is the cause of the births of the inferior, middling, and superior. Such is the form [of the explanation]. (Verse 31)

Thus spoke the other. He understood the words of the other. That which is called pleasure and pain is his; that which is called good and evil is his; that which is wisdom and ignorance, that which is memory and forgetfulness—these are the intertwined events. What is the cause of this? There is wisdom supported by memory, yet it is merely a reflection (*kāśyapi*) and not supported by *vibhava* (the supreme state). Furthermore, if it takes the form of transformation (*vikāra*), such is birth. But memory and wisdom do not truly belong to it; they are merely its support and its ornament. There is another kind of birth that attains *vibhava*, which is clear and pure, devoid of memory and ignorance, and not supported by wisdom. For that [birth] causes [the self] to manifest; there is that which is accumulated through meritorious action (*śubhakarma*) that causes it to manifest. In short, it is forbidden for one who is supported by the distinction of the Self (*ātmaviśeṣa*), for one who possesses wisdom, and for one who possesses memory. This is the way of all kings: there is no longer memory and ignorance; there is only memory, and wisdom is its very form. Such is the lowest, middle, and highest birth, where there is no more memory or ignorance; memory and wisdom alone are their delight, for they are all refined and supported by the distinction of the Self. As you have said, O others, what is the reason it is not so? Thus is the inquiry based on inference: that those supported by the distinction of the Self are few. The name of the Divine Self (*saṅ hyaṅ ātmaviśeṣa*) is wisdom whose essence is the light of memory. Thus is the inference. Birth characterized by memory and ignorance is not supported by memory and wisdom; its movement is likewise not supported by the distinction of the Self. Where is that Self when it is thus? The Self is active even while in the waking state. That which is here is called "knowing" (*maku*); it manifests while not manifesting, it sees while not seeing—that is where it exists. That is why it knows how to manifest in existence and non-existence. Thus is its distinction from the three states of consciousness (*tri-yak*). Those who do not know the distinction, who do not know the scriptures and traditions (*śāstrāgama*), are called those of "blind birth. They are merely possessed of memory, yet they are confused regarding what is good, for they have not mastered the scriptures and traditions. However, if there is a birth that possesses wisdom, is clever, and knows how to study, yet remains at the lowest level because it does not attain wisdom and memory, then it is truly not supported by the distinction of the Self. What then? [The text ends here.]
There is a place; the self has its activity in the fourth stage (tūryapada); that is its place. 32.

Furthermore, there is a birth that is seen as *prajñāna* (supreme wisdom). One who is wise and knows how to act, who possesses no deficiency in any quality, is one of *samyagjñāna* (right knowledge). He is supreme because of his distinction of self (*ātmāviśeṣa*) through *prajñāna*. Now, as for that which is the distinction of self, where is such a place? That which is called the distinction of self is Bhaṭara Dharma; Bhaṭara Dharma is the name of that Self which is without activity in the Fourth State (*tūryapada*). That which is called *prajñāna* serves as the light of instruction. Such a one exists in that place. Furthermore, there is a birth that is seen as *limpad* (the state of being pervaded). By virtue of his excellence, he is able to appropriate both *prajñāna* and *tutur* (instruction). From his excellence, he is called *uttama* (supreme). He is capable of pervading all that is pervasive; he is capable of manifesting inference; he possesses the mastery over wood (*kāṣṭaiśvarya*); and he attains special yogic powers. Because of his excellence, he appropriates the status of a Lord of Yoga (*yogīśvara*), yet he cannot be measured. Bhaṭara Ādipramāṇa exists in such a place; Bhaṭara Ādipramāṇa is the name of Bhaṭara Sadāśivatattva. Beyond even Bhaṭara Dharma, he exists in such a place. 33.

Indeed, there is no differentiation of the *ātman* as inferior, middling, or superior; for all these various births are merely the result of learning (*tutur*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). That which is called the *ātman* is the very essence that pervades everything, capable of attaining the state of supreme bliss. Thus says the *ātman*: "But that *ātman* which exists in the waking state (*jāgrat-pada*), and that *ātman* which exists in the fourth state (*tūryya-pada*), they do not participate in the attainment of supreme bliss. Thus says the principle of the *tambeyan* (the intermediate state): "Now, it is this [intermediate state] that is taken as the *ātman*, along with the inferior, middling, and superior [levels], by which one acquires learning and wisdom. Furthermore, the head and the mind have already been abandoned by him when he takes up the fivefold [elements] from the superior [state]. Learning and wisdom are necessarily embodied when such is the case. Moreover, the *ātman* existing in the waking state and the *ātman* existing in the fourth state are necessarily embodied when such is the case. As long as there is embodiment, so long does it participate in the attainment of supreme bliss when such is the case. Thus spoke the opponent, but it is not so. Here is an analogy: consider a crystal gem (*sphaṭika-maṇi*). Once it has been determined that the crystal gem is purely white, stainless, unobscured, and its color is not yet complete—nevertheless, even though it is thus, one may dye its color red, or blue, or yellow. When the gem possesses that color, it appears to have that color, even though the color is merely a temporary adventitious quality (*avakasan*). This is what is called being "dyed" and "stained. It is as if the color of the gem were lost to perception; the gem's color was indeed not yet complete, having been caused to change by the contact of the gem with the color. But when it is seen again pure, white, and stainless, the gem remains in its original nature, and the red color it previously had has vanished; only its own inherent nature remains. // 34 //

Listen well to this teaching: Thus indeed is the noble Ātman in the waking state (*jāgrapada*), and likewise is the noble Ātman in the fourth state (*tūryapada*). He is the soul of all beings; yet he is subtle, inconceivable, and minute. He is stainless, pure white, unobscured, and not limited. His nature is like the knowledge of crystal. That is why he does not know the objects of the senses; he is the witness who does not tremble. His heart is not exhausted by the burden [of existence], for he is subtle and minute. He is inconceivable and beyond the reach of thought even within the sphere of knowledge. When looking, he does not see; when speaking, he does not speak; when touching, he does not touch—this is his state regarding wind, sound, and sensation. His own form is merely that which is perceived through the senses; that is why it is as if his sensations were empty. To attain the supreme good (*halahayu*) is thus. But furthermore: the Ātman existing in the sleeping state (*sūptapada*) and the Ātman existing in the dreaming state (*svapnapada*) also experience *saṃsāra* and wander among gods, humans, and animals. To attain the supreme good is [the goal]. The "sleeping state" (*sūptapada*) means forgetfulness; it is the cause of the Ātman’s sleep. The "dreaming state" (*svapnapada*) means the Ātman’s wandering while dreaming. The Ātman existing in the sleeping state and the Ātman existing in the dreaming state are what is called *ātmasaṃsāra*. However, the noble Ātman is one; it is only through various distinctions that doubt arises. The Ātman encompasses all principles (*tattva*); it is that which connects them all. Like the surface of a mirror, such is the characteristic of the noble Ātman. It exists in every state. The Ātman is named the "knower" (*hanak*) of the object; it dwells within those states. Now, listen to the characteristics of the noble Ātman as they appear: When he dwells in the dreaming state, his characteristic is that he sees clearly and vividly; he possesses half-knowledge (*tuturardha*) and is endowed with the power of movement (*vurāvutan vaspadā*). His characteristic is like someone looking into a mirror, seeing both things that exist and things that do not exist. When he dwells in the sleeping state, he is unconscious, deluded, and lacks the faculty of knowledge; it is as if the noble Ātman has vanished, for he is overwhelmed by the sleep of time (*kālanidrā*). When he dwells in the waking state, the noble Ātman perceives directly, seeing both things that exist and things that do not exist, because that state is luminous and stainless. His light is the space of color (*varṇṇākāśa*); he is the breath of the winds. Such are the characteristics of the noble Ātman existing in the waking state. The sleeping state, the dreaming state, and the waking state are all moved by the principle of primordial matter (*pradhānatattva*). The name *pradhāna* is the source of all things; it is the cause of the cycle of transmigration (*paracakra*).

Furthermore, it is not defiled by the mind’s conceptualizations; it is purified by the day’s dawn. Now, as for its divisions: one hundred human years constitute one *vṛṅi* (day) in the waking state (*jāgratpada*); twelve human years constitute one *lek* (night) in the waking state; one *yuga* of humans constitutes one year in the waking state; and four *yugas* of humans constitute one *satapa* (century) in the waking state. Such are the characteristics of the divine Self (*ātman*) existing in the waking state. When He resides in the fourth state (*tūryapada*), the divine Self is blissful and tranquil, beholding all things—whether they exist or do not exist. He is supremely blissful in knowing the past, future, and present, because His wisdom (*prajñā*) is the very essence of speech and illumination. His radiance is pure and white, like the color of a crystal gem (*sphaṭika-maṇi*). It is eternal, never failing; it is always day, never obscured by the night’s dawn, nor defiled by the mind’s conceptualizations. However, even the waking state is subject to the cycle of the mind’s conceptualizations. Thus, the waking state is surpassed by the fourth state, because this fourth state is subtle and cannot be grasped by ordinary consciousness. Once the fourth state is realized, it is because our Lord has emerged from that state of the end of the fourth (*tūryāntapada*). His radiance shines forth, like the light of a hundred suns; the difference is that it is not hot. Its illumination is constant, always day, eternally, never obscured by the night’s dawn. He is endowed with omniscience (*arvājñā*), the performer of all deeds, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the power of pervasion (*vibhu-śakti*), the power of lordship (*prabhu-śakti*), and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Such is the surpassing nature of the fourth state by the state of the end of the fourth. Yet, its subtlety and its extreme refinement mean that it can only be known by those who have transcended ordinary consciousness. In short, only those who practice the specific yoga (*yogaviśeṣa*) may reach that place. 35.

Furthermore, it is not possible to describe the state of *tūryapada* and *tūryāntapada*, because they cannot be grasped by consciousness (*citta*). Why is that? Because what is called "consciousness" is the instrument for knowing whether an object exists or does not exist. Thus spoke the opponent. That is why there are three means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) used as a guide for you to attain right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). What are the three means of valid knowledge? They are: direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), inference (*anumānapramāṇa*), and scripture (*āgamapramāṇa*). The objects (*vastu*) are manifold: those seen with the eyes, heard with the ears, and touched by the hands; these are the domain of direct perception. However, those that are subtle (*sūkṣma*), such as the characteristics of *tūryapada*, are the domain of inference. And those that are supremely subtle (*paramasūkṣma*), such as the characteristics of *tūryāntapada*, are the domain of scripture. Such are the characteristics of the states (*pada*): manifold and minute. It is into these that the *ātman* enters; the nature of the *ātman* is manifold and minute. The *ātman* exists in the waking state (*jāgrapada*); this is when the *ātman* is active. It also exists in the deep sleep state (*suptapada*) and in the dream state (*svapnapada*). When one has thoroughly enjoyed the waking state, the *ātman* returns to the *tūryapada*. One truly delights in the *tūryapada*, and from there the *ātman* returns to the *tūryapada*. Such are the characteristics of the divine *ātman* existing within all those subtle levels. 36

The *utpattyakṣa* (the organ of origination) is the head; it is the locus of birth. The noble *ātman* resides in the earth (*pṛthivī*), dwelling within the body of the world (*bhuvanaśarīra*). It is all-pervasive throughout the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*), which are the essence of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*): earth, water, fire, wind, and space. These six together produce the six tastes. Their forms are: sour, astringent, bitter, pungent, salty, and sweet. Sour is the taste of *asem*; astringent is the taste of *sepèt*; bitter is the taste of *pahit*; pungent is the taste of *apḍès*; salty is the taste of *asin*; and sweet is the taste of *manis*. This is what is called the six tastes. They are the first stage in the growth of the body. As for the second stage in the growth of the body: the six tastes consumed by men and women become the essence of what is eaten. That essence produces *rah* (semen) and *dagiṅ* (blood). As for the third stage in the growth of the body: the essence of that *rah* and *dagiṅ* produces *kāmaratih* (erotic desire). This is what is seized by passion (*rāga*). From this, there arises further development: when *kāma* (desire) is predominant over *ratih* (pleasure), it becomes *lanaṅ* (lust); when *ratih* is predominant over *kāma*, it becomes *vadon* (love); when both *kāma* and *ratih* are equal, it becomes *kḍi* (affection). Furthermore, *kāma* produces the anus, the stomach, and the intestines; *ratih* produces *rah* and *dagiṅ*. Such is the manifestation (*vyakti*) of the five great elements, which constitute the root of the body. Their manifestations are: earth as the skin, water as the *rah*, fire as the *dagiṅ*, wind as the intestines, and space as the spinal cord. The five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*) are their essences: the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) becomes the ears; the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*) makes the skin; the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) makes the eyes; the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) makes the tongue; the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) makes the nose. This is what is called the "five spheres" (*pañcagolaka*), which pervade the cosmic egg (*aṇḍabhuvana*), the seven underworlds (*saptapātāla*), and the seven worlds (*saptabhuvana*). The seven worlds are: *bhūrloka* (the feet), *bhuvarloka* (the heart), *svarloka* (the chest), *tapoloka* (the neck), *janarloka* (the lungs), *maharloka* (the nose), and *satyaloka* (the eyes). This is what is called the seven worlds. The seven underworlds are: *Pātāla* (the ankles), *Vaitala* (the heels), *Nitala* (the shins), *Mahātala* (the knees), *Sutala* (the calves), *Talātala* (the insteps), and *Rasātala* (the soles of the feet). This is what is called the seven underworlds. (37)

Indeed, that which is called the "egg-world" (*aṇḍabhuvana*) is the body; it is the birth together with [the elements]. Therein, the seven mountain ranges (*saptaparvata*) are firm; the seven oceans (*saptārṇava*) are overflowing and surging; the seven continents (*saptadvīpa*) are submerged and sunken; and the ten winds (*daśavāyu*) reside within the channels (*nāḍī*). As for the seven mountain ranges: the ridge of Mount Mālyavān; the liver of Mount Niṣadha; the spleen of Mount Gandhamādana; the lungs of Mount Malayamahīdhara; the gallbladder of Mount Triśṛṅga; the heart of Mount Vindhya; and the lungs of Mount Mahāmeru. These are what are called the seven mountain ranges. As for the seven oceans: urine is the lake of feces; semen is the lake of fire; blood is the lake of salt; phlegm is the lake of mud; bile is the lake of honey; marrow is the lake of milk; and the brain is the lake of oil. These are what are called the seven oceans. As for the seven continents: the esophagus is Jambudvīpa; the stomach is Kuśadvīpa; the intestines are Śaṅkhadvīpa; the skin is Śālmalidvīpa; the throat is Gomedhadvīpa; the lungs are Puṣkaradvīpa; and the palate is Krauñcadvīpa. As for the channels (*nāḍī*): they are the tubes of the stomach, their openings at the navel, and they extend upward from the center of the abdomen. There are one hundred and seventy-two of them in total, yet there are ten specific channels among them. Their forms are: Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, Gāndhārī, Hasti, Jihvā, Pūṣā, Alambuṣā, Kuhūh, and Śaṅkhinī. Iḍā is the channel on the right; its function is to know how to exhale through the left nostril. Piṅgalā is the channel on the left; its function is to know how to exhale through the right nostril. Suṣumnā is the one in the middle; its function is to control the breath. Gāndhārī is the channel branching off; its function is to control the wind in the mouth, the eyes, the nose, the ears, and the crown of the head. Hasti is the channel branching off; its function is to control the wind in all the joints, knowing how to exhale through the skin, the pores, and the hair. Jihvā is the channel branching off; its function is to control the wind in the lungs. Pūṣā is the channel branching off; its function is to control the wind in the lungs. Alambuṣā is the channel branching off; its function is to control the wind in the heart and the gallbladder. Kuhūh is the channel branching off; its function is to control the wind in the spleen. Śaṅkhinī is the channel branching off; its function is to control the wind in the ridge and the liver. These are what are called the ten channels. // 38 //

What are the names of the winds that blow? Their types are: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*. The wind called *prāṇa* resides in the heart; it is the master of all the winds, serving as the life-force and the breath. *Apāna* is the wind residing in the anus; it causes the evacuation of what is eaten and drunk, produces desire and pleasure, and its waste becomes feces and urine, while its essence becomes semen. *Udāna* is the wind residing in the throat; it moves the eyes and the nose. *Vyāna* is the wind residing in all the joints; it moves the body and causes aging and death. *Samāna* is the wind residing in the heart; it digests what is eaten and drunk, produces chyme and blood, and generates heat. These are called the five winds (*pañcavāyu*). The ten are as follows: their types are *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkara*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya*. The wind *nāga* performs vomiting. The wind *kūrma* performs the blinking of the eyes and the closing of the eyelids. The wind *devadatta* performs yawning. The wind *kṛkara* performs belching. The wind *dhanañjaya* serves as sound. These are called the ten winds (*daśavāyu*), yet although there are ten in number, their functions are also ten; that is the reason they are called the ten winds. (39)

Thus it is said: there are five *ātman*s, which are the manifestations of the soul (*ātmā*). Their types are: *ātmā*, *parātmā*, *antarātmā*, *sūkṣmātmā*, and *nirātmā*. *Ātmā* is the consciousness residing in the heart; it is the means by which one experiences [objects]. *Parātmā* is the consciousness residing in the eyes; it is the means by which one sees. *Antarātmā* is the consciousness residing in the crown of the head; it is the means by which one distinguishes between waking and sleeping. *Sūkṣmātmā* is the consciousness residing in the ears; it is the means by which one hears. *Nirātmā* is the consciousness residing in the skin; it is the means by which one feels. These are what are called the five *ātman*s; they are the single consciousness that pervades the ten sense organs (*daśendriya*). Their types are: 1. *Śrotrendriya* (the organ of hearing) resides in the ears; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* hears pleasant sounds. 2. *Tvagindriya* (the organ of touch) resides in the skin; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* feels cold and heat, and tastes what is eaten and drunk. 3. *Cakṣurindriya* (the organ of sight) resides in the eyes; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* perceives forms and colors. 4. *Jihvendriya* (the organ of taste) resides in the tongue; it is the cause by which the *ātman* tastes the six flavors. 5. *Ghrāṇendriya* (the organ of smell) resides in the nose; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* smells fragrances, whether sweet or foul. 6. *Vāgindriya* (the organ of speech) resides in the mouth; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* utters words, whether true or false. 7. *Pāṇindriya* (the organ of the hand) resides in the hands; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* grasps. 8. *Pādendriya* (the organ of the foot) resides in the feet; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* walks. 9. *Pāyvīndriya* (the organ of excretion) resides in the anus; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* voids waste and evacuates. 10. *Upasthendriya* (the organ of procreation) resides in the male organ; it is the instrument by which the *ātman* emits semen and blood. Such are the connections of the ten sense organs within the body of the world (*bhuvanaśarīra*). They serve to support the intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), and ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*). The *buddhi* is the instrument by which the *ātman* perceives. The *manas* is the instrument by which the *ātman* forms mental constructs and representations. The *ahaṅkāra* is the instrument by which the *ātman* identifies with objects, and it is also the instrument by which the *ātman* performs virtuous actions. The *buddhi*, *manas*, *ahaṅkāra*, and the ten sense organs are collectively called the thirteen instruments (*trayodaśakaraṇa*). They serve to support the three qualities (*triguṇa*): *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. (40)

The venerable Tripuruṣa: Brahmā is in the *umanděl* (the upper part of the head); Viṣṇu is in the *ampru* (the forehead); Īśvara is in the *pusuhpusuh* (the crown of the head). The positions of the five *ṛṣis* are as follows: Saṅ Kuśika is in the skin of the white hair; Saṅ Garga is in the thick hair; Saṅ Maitrī is in the *vuduk* (the palate); Saṅ Kuruṣya is in the *tahulan* (the spinal column); Saṅ Pṛtañjala is in the marrow of the body. The positions of the *devaṛṣis* are as follows: Saṅ Hyang Maheśvara is in the *vuṅsilan* (the throat); Saṅ Hyang Rudra is in the *dalĕman* (the heart); Saṅ Hyang Śaṅkara is in the *limpa* (the liver); Saṅ Hyang Śambhu is in the *huṇḍuhuṇḍuhan* (the spleen); Saṅ Hyang Sadāśiva is in the *huyuhuyuhan* (the kidneys); Saṅ Hyang Paramaśiva is in the *ḍaḍa* (the lungs). The positions of the seven *ṛṣis* are as follows: Āditya is in the right eye; Soma is in the left eye; Aṅgāra is in the right ear; Budha is in the left ear; Vṛhaspati is in the right nostril; Śukra is in the left nostril; Śaniścara is in the mouth. The positions of the deities (*devatā*) are as follows: Hyang Indra is in the *ḍaḍa*; Hyang Yama is in the right hand; Hyang Varuṇa is in the *valakaṅ* (the left hand); Hyang Kubera is in the left hand; Hyang Vaiśravaṇa is in the center. The positions of the *vidyādharas* and *gandharvas* are as follows: Citrasena is the *kavanin* (the head); Citrāṅgada is the *kaśūran* (the shoulders); Citrarasa is the *kadhīran* (the chest); Gandharva is the *śānta* (the abdomen); he is the *tṛpti* (the satisfaction); the *ramya* (the delight); the *harśśa* (the joy); the *vijah* (the hips); the *kalaṅön* (the feet). Such are the positions of the *sattvas*. O!

And here are the functions of the *rajas* quality: the *dānava* is its cruelty, its ferocity, and its mercilessness; the *daitya* is its anger, its arrogance, and its wickedness; the *rākṣasa* is its delusion, its deceit, its envy, its fickleness, and its recklessness. Such are the functions of the *rajas*. Om.

The functions of the *tamah* (darkness) are as follows: it serves as the *bhūta*, the *yakṣa*, the *kalapa*, the *aṅlih*, the *vaṛg*, the *mtah*, and the *vĕṛ*. The *bhūta* and *piśāca* serve as the *luhya*, the *almĕh*, the *kaluśa*, the *ārip*, the *turu*, and the *puṅguṅ*. Such are the functions of the *tamah*. The functions of the *pada* (states) are as follows: the *jāgrapada* (waking state) is the cause for the *ātman* to be awake at present among humans. The *suptapada* (deep sleep state) is the cause for the *ātman* to be asleep. The *svapnapada* (dreaming state) is the cause for the *ātman* to lie down, to rest, and to be at ease at present among humans. Such are the functions of the *pada*. 41.

What is the *pradhānatattva* (the principle of primordial matter)? It is that which serves as the body of the Lord Ātman; it is called the *amběk*. At present, within the human being, this *amběk* is that which serves as the body of the Lord Ātman at present within the human being. That which is the self (*ātman*) exists within the body at present. Now, what is the name of the body? The *amběk* is the name of the *pradhānatattva*. This *amběk* and the body together are called the *aṅgapradhāna* (the primary constituent) at present within the human being. This is because the *amběk* is deluded regarding the supreme good (*halahayu*). The power of the *amběk* alone is the supreme good. Pleasure and pain are experienced by the human being through the *amběk*. It is from the *amběk* alone that objects of sense arise, having the ten faculties (*daśendriya*) as their means (*sādhana*) and the ten paths (*daśamārgga*) as their gates. Its hand reaches out toward the objects (*iṣaya*) within the *aṇḍabhuvana* (the cosmic egg). It perceives those who possess the *nipuṇatattva* (the subtle principle, i.e., the *triguṇatattva*). Such is the sequence. Therefore, the ten faculties must be directed toward their respective objects and withdrawn back into the *amběk*. The *amběk* withdraws the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The Lord is the *pramāṇa*. Next, the specific qualities (*dharmaviśeṣa*). From the specific qualities, one withdraws the internal distinctions (*antaviśeṣa*). From the internal distinctions, one withdraws the infinite distinctions (*anantaviśeṣa*). When he has finished withdrawing them into the infinite distinctions, that is the purpose of the *prayogasandhi* (the junction of application), understood by the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*). As for this *prayogasandhi*, it cannot exist without the guidance of *samyagjñāna* (right knowledge). Those who understand the *prayogasandhi* do so without a cause other than *samyagjñāna*. It cannot exist without the foundation (*bhūmi*) of observances (*vrata*), austerity (*tapa*), yoga, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). In short: with observances, austerity, yoga, and meditative absorption as its foundation, with *samyagjñāna* as its guide, and with the *prayogasandhi* as its means, he alone is capable of attaining the particularity of the Lord. It is like a tree planted in the ground: once the sap has reached it, the tree will surely flourish. There are indeed those who plant the tree but do not wait for the Lord; they do not see its flourishing. There is a reason for such behavior: they have missed the path. The meaning is this: there are those who undertake these observances, austerities, yoga, and meditative absorption, yet they fail to perfect the *prayogasandhi*. Because of this, they miss right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Even though their practice is sharp, because they lack the intensity (*tīkṣṇa*) and the means (*sādhana*) to produce meditative absorption, they remain ignorant of the reach of their own knowledge. This is because they do not know the knowledge of the heart (*hṛdayajñāna*) and lack the guidance of *samyagjñāna*. It is certain that the end of such a practitioner of yoga is failure. The fruit of such observances merely leads to experiencing pleasure and seeking enjoyment; the Lord Ātman merely goes to the heavenly realm (*svarga*).

Thus it is: the fruit of *samādhi* is that one protects the fruit of *vrata*. Once the fruit of *vrata* has been enjoyed by the *ātman* in heaven, the noble *ātman* descends again. It takes birth in the world of humans; it becomes a king and is wealthy. Its birth is one of merit (*kṛtapuṇya*). Such is the nature of humanity: it is characterized by memory and forgetfulness. At the time when there is memory, the virtuous conduct (*śīla*) produced by that birth remains. At the time when there is forgetfulness, the evil conduct produced by that birth remains. Thus, one may fall into heaven, hell, the human realm, or the animal realm. Such is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a person who lacks right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). 42

Now, as for that person who possesses the knowledge of action (*vyāpārajñāna*), though it is profound, his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from past acquisitions have been severed; he is one who seeks to attain *samyagjñāna* (perfect knowledge) itself. This is precisely why he takes the stages of *vrata*, *tapa*, *yoga*, and *samādhi*; for without these, *samyagjñāna* cannot exist, nor can there be *samādhi* without its causal signs (*nimitta*). What are these signs? Here is their sequence: The qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* do not yet manifest clearly. One should cultivate what is good and practice the dharma of merit (*puṇya*). Such is the description of *sattva*. Anger, gluttony, and pride are the description of *rajas*. Deceit, impurity, drinking intoxicants, and constant restlessness are the description of *tamas*. Thus, while *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are present, they do not manifest clearly. *Rajas* and *tamas* are the source of their own nature; *sattva* is luminosity (*prakāśa*), characterized by mature wisdom (*prajñā*). Remembering the reality of the three qualities (*triguṇatattva*)—this is the sequence. That is why *rajas* and *tamas* are suppressed within *samādhi* through the means (*sādhana*) of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), with the mind, intellect, and ego (*citta-buddhi-manas*) as companions. When the day is peaceful and calm, free from obscurations and not yet fully complete, the knowledge of the head becomes stainless; the self (*ātman*) of *rajas* and *tamas* becomes pleasant, and the person enters deeply into *sattva*. Luminosity resides in *sattva*. This is the principle of the power of wisdom arising from *samādhi*. As long as that wisdom is attained, perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) will gradually emerge through the mastery of the Lord of Yoga (*yogīśvara*). Perfect knowledge understands the junction of the application (*prayogasandhi*), taking the stages of *vrata*, *tapa*, *yoga*, and *samādhi* as its foundation. It rests upon and is embraced by the excellence of yoga, serving as the lamp for perfect knowledge. With the application of the junction as its means, and the stages of *vrata*, *tapa*, *yoga*, and *samādhi* as its foundation, the junction of the application is like a bow drawn back, while perfect knowledge is like the arrowhead. The stages of *vrata*, *tapa*, *yoga*, and *samādhi* are like the bow-handle, which, when released, propel the junction of the application, causing the arrow of perfect knowledge to fly forth and the essence of *vrata*, *tapa*, *yoga*, and *samādhi* to reach their goal. //0// 43

This is the *prayogasandhi*. What is its meaning? *Prayogasandhi* means the method (*upāya*). Its forms are: *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, *tarka*, and *samādhi*. All these together are called *sandhi*. It is the very consciousness (*cetana*) that becomes intensely luminous, becoming one, not dependent on others, steadfast, firm, and unmoving; it is the state of the four meditations (*caturdhyāna*). What are the four meditations? Their forms are: while standing, eating, walking, and sleeping. Standing: the Lord remains seated. Eating: the Lord eats. Walking: the Lord walks. Sleeping: the Lord sleeps. In short, the Lord Himself follows along with whatever state a person may be in; for that which is called "following" (*tutur*) is the Lord’s manifestation within the body at this stage of *sakala*. Furthermore, there is *āsana* (posture). Its forms are: *padmāsana*, *vajrāsana*, *paryaṅkāsana*, *svastikāsana*, *vidyāsana*, and *daṇḍāsana*. These are the six types of *āsana*; they are unified in their essence, and thus one should choose and adopt them. When the practitioner of *prayogasandhi* has finished sitting, he should then cause the Divine Life-force (*saṅ hyaṅ urip*) to settle into a single-pointed mind (*ekacitta*). Once the Divine Life-force has settled, he performs *prāṇāyāma*. There is a method of breath-control called *pamaśeḥ* (the purifier). Its forms are: *recaka* (exhalation), *pūraka* (inhalation), and *kumbhaka* (retention). *Recaka*: One should expel the aforementioned air from the mouth. Then, contract the left nostril, close it, and then open it. Then, inhale the air; that is called *pūraka*. *Kumbhaka*: After the air has been inhaled, one closes the mouth, contracts the nostrils, and closes them. One should keep the gaze fixed on the eye-entrance (*netradvāra*). If one is not yet practiced, one should fix the gaze on the nose. One must breathe slowly and gently so as not to snore. This practice of opening the nostrils should continue for seven days. If it becomes difficult, one should relax the contraction of the nostrils. The purpose of *prāṇāyāma* is to suppress passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), and to bring about the light of *sattva*. Furthermore, the body must not become too heavy. Furthermore, there is another method of *kuñcī* (contraction) which does not involve expelling the air. In brief, it is simply holding the breath. However, one should perform *recaka* and *kumbhaka* as before. This is the secret *kuñcī* that should be practiced. In brief, it is the very consciousness that becomes intensely luminous. One should direct it toward the *kadalīpuṣpa* (the lotus of the heart). That is the place where his bliss resides. It resonates within the heart, vibrating through the inner organ (*antahkaraṇa*). Thus, this is called performing the *prāṇasandhi-jāti*. That is what is meant by *pūjājāti*: a subtle offering to the Divine.

Furthermore, when it is thus sharpened by means of non-concentration (asamādhi), the manifest group of vital airs (vāyu-gaṇa) disappears; it becomes absorbed within its own source, because the individual consciousness (tañcinetana) is [unified] with the Self (ātman). Such is the path called the "Secret Key" (kuñcī-rahasya). 44.

Next is *pratyāhārayoga*. It means withdrawing all the senses from their respective objects; the *citta*, *buddhi*, and *manas* are restrained so that they do not engage with one another, and the *cittālila* (the play of consciousness) is restrained. This is what is called *pratyāhārayoga*. That knowledge which is not dependent on others, which is without modification (*vikāra*), which is pleasant in its state of being, which shines forth without obstruction—this is what is called *dhyānayoga*. Closing all the gates: the nostrils, the mouth, the wind of the breath (*vāyu*) within the nose, and the *vunvunan* (the crown of the head). However, if one does not practice the *vāyu*, it will not enter there; it remains in the nostrils, and the movement of the *vāyu* is obstructed. This is what is called *prāṇāyāmayoga*. There is the sound of *oṃkāra* dwelling within the heart; this is *dhāraṇā*. It is the support for the *kaṛṅö* (the inner self) at the time of *yoga*; this is what is called *śūnya*. When it is thus, the Lord Śiva is the *śivātmā* (the self of Śiva); this is what is called *dhāraṇayoga*. Indeed, space (*ākāśa*) is the Supreme Reality (*paramārtha*), yet it is beyond the *ātman*. There is no sound in it; that is understood as the *paramārtha*. It is beyond all fluctuations (*avaṅavaṅ*). It is the state of total stillness (*alilaṅ*). This is what is called *tarkkayoga*. That knowledge which is not indifferent, not forgetful, in which there is no arrogance, in which there is nothing to be meditated upon, which is still and not subject to disappearance, which has no obstructions, and in which the conscious principle (*cetana*) is not a mere material thing—because it enters and awakens the body, transcending the four conceptualizations (*caturkalpanā*). What are the four conceptualizations? All of these do not exist for the *yogīśvara*. When the *citta* dwells comfortably within the heart, it is said to have "returned to the womb" (*mulih riṅ ambĕk*). This is the primordial state of consciousness established and supported by what is called the "womb. It is the source of the teachings, the root of excellence. Thus he spoke: "The womb is that which dissolves the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How does the womb dissolve the means of valid cognition? It is as follows: the *citta*, *buddhi*, and *manas* are withdrawn from their various functions and become like the light of the teachings, resembling a crystal (*sphaṭika*). Just as a crystal gem is clear when its sharpness is intact, this is called *sphaṭikajñāna*. When the light of the divine *sphaṭikajñāna* is fully manifest, it perceives all principles (*sarvatattva*) along with good and evil karma (*śubhāśubhakarmma*). By perceiving the good and evil karma and all principles, the divine *sphaṭikajñāna* ascends to the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*). When it dwells there comfortably, it perceives that all principles and [karma] have been reduced to ashes (*bhasmībhūta*) through its realization.

Whatever pure or impure karma resides within me, I offer it into the fire-pit (kuṇḍa); this is called the Mahāhoma. By means of this, all afflictions (kleśas) without exception are extinguished; this is what is known as Dhāraṇāyoga. // 45 //

The consciousness (cetanā) is established within the monkey (kapiṅtiga). Its characteristic is this: the *oṃkāra* or *praṇava* resides in the heart; because it is dissolved into the *śivatattva*, its characteristic is that the mind (*citta*) is withdrawn, having transcended the primary and secondary limbs (*aṅgapradhāna*). It remains with a single-pointed mind even in the subtle state, possessing the mouth of the *tūryapada*; thus, he knows the distinction through direct experience. He is like a snake that has slithered into a bamboo tube—neither moving nor coiling, but remaining still and fixed. Such is the outward appearance of his knowledge as he maintains a one-pointed mind, possessing the mouth of the *tūturya* (the fourth state), at the limit of his knowledge of the joints (*sandhijñāna*). Indeed, he sleeps soundly when asleep, for he possesses the mouth of the waking state (*jāgrapada*). How is the waking state attained together with the *tūryapada*? The deity is unified and mixed with meditation (*dhyāna*). Indeed, the consciousness (*tutur*) is the space (*ākāśa*) of the awakening of the Lord Pradhāna, emerging from the primary and secondary limbs; this is called *abhisandhi*. It is the separation of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the cessation of the consciousness and forgetfulness of the Lord Ātmā; this is further called *dharmaviśeṣa*. Possessing the mouth of the seven limbs (*saptāṅga*) and the seven nectars (*saptāmṛta*), he is scorched by the seven fires (*saptāgni*). The seven limbs are: Puruṣa, Sattva, Rajas, Yama (restraint), Buddhi, Manas, and Ahaṅkāra. The seven nectars are: Sound, Touch, Form, Taste, Smell, Knowledge (*kinavruhan*), and Volition (*sinaṅkalpa*). The seven fires are: Seeing, Hearing, Tasting, Smelling, Speaking, Thinking (*mamastvani*), and Imagining (*mamikalpa*). If the seven limbs are known and serve as the mouth of the Lord of Yoga (*yogīśvara*), they are the cause of his body being complete with the sense of taste (*rāsana*), free from obstacles, and free from old age and death. If the seven nectars are known and serve as his life-force, they are the cause of the youth of the Lord of Yoga, whose lifespan does not diminish along with his birth. If the seven fires are known and he is scorched by them, they are the cause of the Lord of Yoga becoming pervasive (*vyāpin*) and all-encompassing (*vyāpaka*), capable of fulfilling every desire regarding the manifest world (*sakala*), for we, the Lords, are called the seven fires. Therefore, the Lord of the Seven Fires consumes those seven limbs and seven nectars, for they produce afflictions (*upasarga*). Affliction means the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) that cling to the body of the Self (*ātman*). Here is an illustration: it is like a bamboo tube filled with ginger; the ginger is the source of the bamboo, yet it occupies the interior of the bamboo.

It is just as when a piece of iron becomes wet with gold; such is the nature of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), which cling to the body of the self (*ātman*). Therefore, it does not fall away by means of *samādhi* alone. Friend, this is what is called a hindrance (*upasarga*) by the Lord of Yogins; now, listen to the manner in which these hindrances appear: 46.

Furthermore, there may appear those resembling Gandharvas, or those resembling Vidyādharas; these are humans who have appeared before the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*) during the time of yoga. Moreover, there are formless deities (*marūpa-devatā*) who ascend upon the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*) and seek to disturb the mind of the Lord of Yogins; furthermore, there are Ṛṣis who arrive, offering worship with a rain of flowers, or perhaps seeking the meaning of the sacred teachings (*ājña*). Yet, the Lord of Yogins remains undisturbed during the time of yoga. Such occurrences are *sattvopasarga* (obstacles caused by sentient beings) encountered by the Lord of Yogins. Furthermore, if one sees [visions] such as being pursued, being chased, or being pulled about; or appearing like a madman; or appearing to fly through the sky—these are the physical forms of Dānavas, Daityas, or Rākṣasas that disturb the *samādhi* of the Lord of Yogins. Such occurrences are *rajopasarga* (obstacles caused by passion). Furthermore, if the body of the Lord of Yogins becomes agitated during the time of yoga—such as trembling, sweating profusely, yawning, or feeling as if being pierced in the heart; or experiencing forgetfulness and confusion as if consciousness were vanishing—these are the efforts of sleepiness and darkness encountered by the Lord of Yogins during such times. Moreover, if one becomes attached to the state of yoga, these obstacles (*upasarga*) will become a source of fear. There is indeed evil karma that brings about these results, which cause the Lord of Yogins to feel weary and distressed, thereby causing his *samādhi* to waver. Then there is the Holy Seven Fires (*saptāgni*). Even they are surpassed by the brilliance of this *samādhi*, which possesses the mouth of all-knowing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) and performs all deeds. When the Holy Seven Fires are within this *samādhi*, they are consumed and reduced to ashes by the power of the obstacles. When the Holy Seven Fires are ignited within the *samādhi*, they are consumed and reduced to ashes by the power of the obstacles. When the Lord of Yogins is ignited, he becomes free from veils (*nirāvaraṇa*), never again to fall back, like the clarity of the sky. This is what is called *tarkayoga*. 47.

Beyond the *antaviśeṣa* (the limit of differentiation) exists the Holy Self (*ātman*) which is thus. It exists together with the Lord *Sadāśivatattva*, who is omniscient (*sarvajña*), the performer of all actions (*sarvakāryakartṛ*), and possesses the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the power of pervasion (*vibhuśakti*), the power of lordship (*prabhuśakti*), and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). He is free from the latent impressions of the ripening of karma (*karmavipākāśaya*). Regarding the *Sadāśivatattva*: what is meant by "the ripening of karma" (*karmavipāka*)? "Karma" refers to good and evil deeds; "ripening" (*vipāka*) refers to the experience of their fruits within the body; and "latent impression" (*āśaya*) refers to the remainder that continues to produce further karma for the self. This is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*). If the habitual tendency of that prior karma is evil, it causes the person to perform evil deeds in vain; if the habitual tendency of that prior karma is good, it causes the person to perform good deeds in vain. There is nothing at all that remains as a latent impression for the self; this is what is meant by being "free from the latent impressions of the ripening of karma. This is called the state of being liberated from good and evil. That is the *Sadāśivatattva*. Thus ends the fourth level of consciousness established and residing [within]. The fifth level of consciousness is the most excellent. Its description is as follows: the Holy One of Distinction (*Viśeṣa*), who has transcended the limit of distinction (*antaviśeṣa*). How does He transcend the limit of distinction? He is the state of the Fourth Beyond (*tūryyāntapada*), which is the very object of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). What is meant by the "state of the Fourth Beyond"? It is beyond duality (*rva*). Duality means non-existence, meaning absence. Its definition is: uncuttable, not to be cut; the subtlest of the subtle, the most minute of the minute; beyond all worldly activities. It is the state of being omniscient and the performer of all actions, yet it is purely purposeless and does not function. It is without beginning, without end, without activity, and remains eternally in a state of stillness. This is called "Samādhi-yoga," because *samādhi* is the ultimate goal of all spiritual practices (*sādhana*). Such is the abiding state of the Lord *Sadāśivatattva*; this is what is meant by "having transcended the limit of distinction. 48.

Furthermore, such is the nature of this *samādhi* which is attained by the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*). It becomes manifest when he has mastered the eightfold sovereignty (*kāṣṭaiśvarya*) over all things. What is meant by "eightfold sovereignty"? It is the attainment of specific yogic powers (*yogaviśeṣa*) through intense meditation; there are eight such perfections (*siddhi*), namely: *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *mahimā*, *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, and *yatrakāmāvasāyitva*. *Aṇimā* means that the body of the Lord of Yogins is exceedingly small, subtle, and minute. Because of this, the Lord of Yogins is able to enter into others; he cannot be obstructed by mountains or stones, and he can even vanish into the earth. There is nothing that his sovereign power cannot penetrate; this is called *aṇimā*. *Laghimā* means that the body of the Lord of Yogins is light and soft like cotton wool. Because of this, the Lord of Yogins can travel through the sky, reach the heavens, traverse the intermediate space, and be able to see the gods (*vvai*). This is called *laghimā*. *Mahimā* means that he is great in other lands, honored, worshipped, and revered with devotion. He is not surpassed by anyone else; this is called *mahimā*. *Prāpti* means that whatever object he desires, he attains it without difficulty; this is called *prāpti*. *Prākāmya* means that he is able to assume various forms—whether young, old, large, or small—and he is able to enter the consciousness of all beings; this is called *prākāmya*. *Īśitva* means that he travels to the celestial realms (*svarga*) and is honored and adored by all the gods (*devatā*). He is able to create the gods within his own realm, and no god can surpass him, for the Lord (Śiva) himself resides within the body of the Lord of Yogins. This is called *īśitva*. *Vaśitva* means that there is nothing he cannot overcome, and he is never hindered by his own will; this is called *vaśitva*. *Yatrakāmāvasāyitva* means that he is able to create the gods as his own subjects. There is nothing he cannot overcome and he is never hindered; he is able at will to transform a god into a human or a human into a god. This is called *yatrakāmāvasāyitva*. (49)

This is what is called attaining *kāṣṭaiśvarya* (the sovereignty of wood). It is the sign of one who has already carried out the specific yoga (*yogaviśeṣa*). For "not being burned" means that when there is a fire, he is not burned. That which is called *kalpasen* (endurance through the cosmic age) is seen as its sign even now. One who attains *kalpasen* cannot be harmed by those who have already attained the signs of having carried out the specific yoga. What causes the Lord of Yoga (*yogīśvara*) to be neither burnt nor released? Because he has already attained the specific yoga; his name is "already accomplished. He is able to be all-pervasive (*vyāpī*, *vyāpaka*) throughout everything at this time. He is able to cause his own life to cease; he can cause the primary elements (*aṅgapradhāna*) to cease. No karma whatsoever can affect the Lord of Yoga, because all of that has already been exhausted during the stage of yoga (*yogapada*). That is the reason why no karma can affect the Lord of Yoga. Should others speak thus, it is merely the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*). Those have already been exhausted previously during the stage of yoga. Only the latent impression of goodness (*sattva*) enters into the Lord of Yoga, for such is his very nature. For the fruit of the *buddhi-sattva* is what brings the Lord of Yoga back [to life]. As for the fruit of the *buddhi-rajah*, it is indeed the fruit of the *buddhi-sattva* that serves as the vehicle for the Lord of Yoga. Once that has been enjoyed by the Lord of Yoga, it is then discarded by him. He makes it his own, he takes hold of it, he seizes victory and makes it his own possession. He gives it to him as the vehicle of the sovereignty of wood. When the latent impression of *sattva* is discarded by the Lord of Yoga, then, when the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) dissolve, he returns to his own state (*asthiti*) again and again. Such is the Lord of Yoga; he remembers and speaks only [of this], returning to his own body together with the Lord Paramaśiva-tattva, using the *prayogasandhi* as the means, with the stages of vow (*vrata*), austerity (*tapas*), yoga, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as the ground. // 50 //

Thus concludes the *Saṅ hyaṅ Tattvajñāna* (The Sacred Knowledge of Reality) and the *Saṅ hyaṅ Prayogasandhi* (The Sacred Application of the Junctions). Completed. O! This is the culmination of *samyagjñāna* (right knowledge). O!
